body:
When I started working on websites, I didn’t expect to spend so much time figuring out why something wasn’t working. You change a setting, check the website, and everything looks good. Then you open it on your phone and the banner is cropped, a button is missing, or something that worked five minutes ago suddenly looks different.

That’s been a big part of my experience: trying things, getting stuck, asking questions, and working through the problem. I’m Javier Sibauste originally from Panama moved to U.S.A and joined the University of Palm Beach State College and currently living in Poland. I am the person behind Sibauste Systems. My background is in network administration and security, but my work has taken me into websites, online stores, analytics, integrations, and all the little technical details that come with them.

I like working on a bit of everything. Sometimes I’m improving a page, sometimes I’m checking store settings, and sometimes I’m trying to understand why two tools aren’t communicating properly. For my first blog post, I wanted to share a little about that experience and give credit to Codex, which has been working with me along the way.

## Some of the Websites I’ve Been Working On

These are some of the websites that have been part of my work and learning:

* sibavitamin.com
* sibavitamin.co
* my-pets.pl
* demisalon.pl
* holisha.pl

My involvement has been different with each project. Depending on what was needed, I’ve worked on website changes, troubleshooting, store settings, or the tools connected behind the scenes. Each project has given me something new to figure out. A pet store, a beauty business, and a vitamin store have different needs, even when some of the technical work overlaps. I’d like to share more about these projects in future posts: what I worked on, what gave me trouble, and what I learned from it.

## Shopify: A Lot Happens Behind the Store

A lot of my practical experience has come from working with Shopify.

At first, it’s easy to focus on how the store looks. But once you start working on it regularly, you realize how much happens behind the pages customers see. There are products, shipping settings, apps, tracking, Google tools, and connections to other sales channels. Getting those pieces to work together takes attention.

I’ve worked on storefront changes, product and catalog connections, analytics checks, and troubleshooting. Sometimes the challenge is making an improvement. Other times, it’s finding the setting that explains why something is behaving strangely. One thing I’ve learned is to slow down before deciding what caused a problem.

If people visit a store but don’t buy, for example, there could be several explanations. I want to look at the available information and understand where customers might be getting stuck before changing things.

That investigation is something I enjoy. It can be frustrating while you’re in the middle of it, but finding the cause—and seeing the improvement afterward makes it worthwhile.

## Wix: The Small Details Add Up

Working with Wix has made me pay more attention to the whole experience of using a website.

I’ve worked on navigation, store content, language settings, and the wording customers see while shopping. On a website for Polish customers, for example, changing the language setting was only part of the job. There were still individual labels and messages to inspect.

That sounds like a small thing, but imagine browsing a store in Polish and suddenly finding part of the cart in English. It can make the website feel unfinished or confusing. So I’ve been getting into the habit of following the process as a customer would. Can I find what I’m looking for? Does the menu make sense? Are the labels clear? What happens when I open it on my phone?

I’ve also learned to pay close attention to drafts and published changes. Before editing, I want to know which version I’m working on. Afterward, I want to check what actually changed.

## WordPress and WooCommerce: Still Learning, Still Exploring

WordPress and WooCommerce are also part of what I’m learning. I have more hands-on examples to share from Shopify and Wix right now, and I’m comfortable saying that. I don’t want to make it sound like I have the same level of experience with every platform.

Even setting up my own website brought me into WordPress.com, because that’s where I purchased my domain. Connecting it to GitHub Pages meant working through DNS records, domain verification, HTTPS, and Google Search Console. There were a few moments of, “Okay, I followed the steps… so why is there still an error?”

Working through those moments helped me understand how the services connect. It also showed me how useful it is to have your own project where you can practice and learn. As I build more experience with WordPress and WooCommerce, I’ll have more to share here.

## My Own Website Became a Project of Its Own

Building Sibauste Systems gave me somewhere to bring my ideas together.

I started with a few design drafts and a lot of ideas. I knew the feeling I wanted, but I wasn’t completely sure how to turn it into a working website. The *Adam and computer* banner became a big part of that. I liked the idea of showing a human reaching toward a computer. It connected with the inspiration behind the site and the kind of work I enjoy.

**Then came the adjustments.**

Move the box because it’s covering the computer’s face. Make Adam easier to see. Fix the banner on mobile. Make the green lights a little bigger. Figure out why the animation moves on my phone but seems stuck on my computer. Those were actual things I noticed while using the website.

It took a few rounds, but that process helped me make the site feel more like mine. It also taught me that checking a website on one screen is never enough.

## I Have to Give Codex Some Credit

I’ve been working with OpenAI’s Codex throughout this process, and I want to give that collaboration proper credit. Codex has helped me turn ideas into code, understand errors, make changes, and work through technical setups that were new to me. We’ve worked on responsive layouts, mobile navigation, animations, the contact form, GitHub publishing, and the blog you’re reading now.

We also set up the blog editor behind Cloudflare Access. That gave me a better understanding of how access protection works and the difference between protecting the editor and keeping files in a repository private. Another part of the process was dealing with dependency alerts. We checked the affected packages, updated the sanitizer used by the blog, and ran the tests and build before publishing the update.

I appreciate having that help. I can explain an idea in my own words, ask why something happened, and work through the next step. Sometimes that means asking the same thing a different way until I understand it. That’s part of learning too. 

**As an** entrepreneur, I really implore everyone to see AI as a tool for learning and improving **their** knowledge. **AI** can be very handy and do the **entire job**, but **for me, it's like**: what is the point of letting **AI do everything** if I am not going to learn anything?..... 

## How I Use AI in My Work

Working with Codex has become a mix of building, troubleshooting, and learning.

Sometimes I know exactly what I want and need help putting it together. Other times, I’m looking at an error message and trying to figure out where to start. Along the way, I’ve been practicing skills such as reading and adjusting HTML, CSS, and JavaScript; working with Git and GitHub; configuring hosting and domains; checking integrations; and testing changes before publishing them.

I’m also learning to ask better questions....or improving my **PROMPT**!!!

What is causing the error? What will this change affect? How can I check whether it worked? Is there something I’m assuming without enough evidence? AI is useful to me because I can work through those questions while doing the project. I still need to review the changes and check the result.

If we fix the mobile layout, I want to open it on my phone. If a form is supposed to send a request, I want to understand where that request goes. If an editor is supposed to require a login, I want to know what someone sees when they aren’t signed in.

I realized that I need to know exactly what I am building and why. If I want the AI to build it efficiently using fewer tokens while clearly explaining the process, the prompt must be as precise and well guided as possible. That’s a habit I want to keep developing.

## What I Want This Blog to Be

I want this blog to feel like a place where I can share what I’m actually doing.

Some posts will be about website projects. Others might cover a technical problem, a platform I’m exploring, an integration, or something I’ve learned while using AI tools. I’m still building my experience, and I don’t expect that learning to stop. That’s also how I’m approaching Sibauste Systems. I enjoy helping with website problems, store improvements, tracking, integrations, and those technical details that can become frustrating when you’re trying to run a business.

For now, this post is my introduction. If you’ve ever spent an hour searching for a setting that was right in front of you the whole time, we probably already have something in common.

[Want a similar optimized setup for your e-commerce store? Check out my web development services.](https://sibaustesystem.com)

*Written by Javier Sibauste.*
